title: De lineis curvis non in eodem plano sitis, quae maximi minimive proprietate sunt praeditae

deep.reconstruction:
Context: E740 looks for space curves that make an integral ∫ w(v) ds extremal, where v is the distance from a fixed centre (v² = x²+y²+z²). The earlier sections showed that the extremal lies in a plane z = my + nx through the centre. They also introduced α=(mm+1)/√(mm+nn+1), β=mn/√(mm+nn+1), γ=√(mm+nn+1) and δ=√((mm+1)/(mm+nn+1)), and wrote x = δv cos φ and αy+βx = δv sin φ. In effect, (x, αy+βx)/δ are orthonormal coordinates in that plane, so v and φ are plane polar coordinates. Likewise tan ψ = αp+β (with p = dy/dx) is the inclination of the tangent in those coordinates. The Euler–Lagrange equation from §37 is dψ + (w′v/w) dφ = 0.

§38 eliminates x and y by differentiating the two polar relations. Dividing one differential by the other, and using dy = p dx, gives tan ψ = (dv sin φ + v dφ cos φ)/(dv cos φ − v dφ sin φ). This is the standard tangent-angle formula in polar coordinates.

§39, the 'praecipuum artificium': set v dφ = t dv. Then tan ψ = (tan φ + t)/(1 − t tan φ), the tangent of a sum of angles, so ψ = φ + arctan t. Here arctan t is the angle χ between the radius vector and the tangent. Differentiating, dψ = dφ + dt/(1+t²). Substituting into the principal equation gives (w′v/w) dφ + dφ + dt/(1+t²) = 0. Euler remarks that this alone gains little, because t still hides second differentials and three variables (v, φ, t) are involved.

Next page: substitute dφ = t dv/v and divide by t. This gives dw/w + dv/v + dt/(t(1+t²)) = 0. It integrates to w v t/√(1+t²) = C, i.e. w(v)·v·sin χ = C. That is the Bouguer/Clairaut invariant, the analogue of angular momentum for a central field. A final quadrature follows: dφ = C dv/(v√(w²v² − C²)). Together with the new integration constant there are four constants: C, m, n and the constant of φ.
errors: No mathematical errors on this page. The derivation of tan ψ and the angle-addition step are correct.
'veriabilis' is a misprint for 'variabiles' in the original edition; it is not a transcription error.

ideas.what: Tangent inclination in polar coordinates: tan ψ = (dv sin φ + v dφ cos φ)/(dv cos φ − v dφ sin φ); with t = v dφ/dv this gives ψ = φ + arctan t, where arctan t is the angle between radius and tangent
ideas.modern_name: Polar tangent angle; angle between radius vector and tangent (tan χ = r dθ/dr)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Standard 17th–18th c. differential geometry (Newton, the Bernoullis, Euler)
ideas.where_published: Euler's Introductio in analysin infinitorum vol. II and the Methodus inveniendi (1744), plane central problems

ideas.what: Reduction of the Euler–Lagrange equation for ∫ w(v) ds to the first integral w v sin χ = C and then to a quadrature dφ = C dv/(v√(w²v²−C²))
ideas.modern_name: Bouguer's invariant / Clairaut relation; conservation of angular momentum for a radially symmetric metric or refractive index n(r)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (Methodus inveniendi 1744, plane case); Bouguer and Clairaut in other contexts; Johann Bernoulli for refraction analogies
ideas.where_published: Methodus inveniendi lineas curvas (E65), chapter on curves with radial weight functions; in space form, E740 itself (published 1813)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a careful but standard reduction: it uses the polar tangent angle and obtains the classical first integral w v sin χ = const. These are well-known results, known to Euler from his 1744 work. The only non-planar aspect, that the extremal lies in a plane through the centre, belongs to earlier pages and is also standard.
transcription_corrections: The transcription matches the image. The original prints 'veriabilis' (misprint for 'variabiles'), and the formula on line 5 is printed with a smudge as 'αy + βx = δ v sin. φ'.
